## Welcome {#home}

### Poliomyelitis

**Learning Objectives:**

- Describe poliovirus, its reservoir, and modes of transmission
- Classify the clinical spectrum of polio infection
- Recognize the features of paralytic poliomyelitis
- Compare IPV and OPV — mechanism, advantages, and complications
- Explain AFP surveillance and vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV)
- Outline India's path to polio-free certification

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
Polio is a landmark eradication success story — India was certified
polio-free in 2014 after being one of the last endemic reservoirs. This
module pairs the biology with the surveillance/vaccination programme
that achieved that result.
:::

---

## Agent, Reservoir, and Transmission {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Agent:** poliovirus (RNA virus), 3 serotypes — most paralytic outbreaks
are **type 1**. **Reservoir:** humans only, no chronic carriers, no
animal source. Most infections are **subclinical** — for every clinical
case there may be ~1,000 subclinical infections in children, driving
silent community spread.

**Transmission:** primarily **faeco-oral** (contaminated water, food,
fingers, flies); droplet spread can occur during the acute phase and
matters more where sanitation is already good.

**Incubation period:** 7–14 days (range 3–35 days). Most vulnerable age
in India: **6 months–3 years**.

---

## Clinical Spectrum {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Only about **1% of infections** involve the CNS and cause paralysis —
the rest fall into three non-paralytic categories:

| Form | Features |
|---|---|
| **Inapparent (subclinical)** | No symptoms; detected only by virus isolation or rising antibody titre |
| **Abortive polio** | Mild, self-limiting illness from viraemia; not clinically distinguishable without lab tests |
| **Non-paralytic polio** | Neck/back stiffness and pain, synonymous with aseptic meningitis; recovery in 2–10 days |
| **Paralytic polio** | Virus invades the CNS — see next slide |

---

## Paralytic Polio: Recognition {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Asymmetrical flaccid paralysis** is the hallmark, preceded by fever
  at onset
- Paralysis is **descending** (hip → distal limb), asymmetric and
  patchy, with proximal muscles more affected than distal
- Progresses to its maximum in under 4 days (up to 4–7); deep tendon
  reflexes diminish before paralysis onset; **no sensory loss**
- Bulbar/bulbospinal forms involve cranial nerves — facial asymmetry,
  swallowing difficulty; **respiratory insufficiency is the usual cause
  of death**

**No specific treatment exists** — management is supportive: good
nursing care and early physiotherapy to minimize residual disability.

---

## IPV vs. OPV {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

| | IPV (Salk) | OPV (Sabin) |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Inactivated, injectable | Live attenuated, oral |
| **Immunity induced** | Humoral only (IgG/IgM/IgA in serum) | Humoral **and** intestinal (secretory IgA) |
| **Herd effect** | None — doesn't block gut transmission | Strong — vaccine virus spreads to contacts, achieving herd immunity at ~66% coverage |
| **Epidemic use** | Poor fit — needs multiple doses, injections risky during outbreaks | Well suited — rapid, can interrupt transmission |
| **Key risk** | None significant | Rare **Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP)**, mostly linked to Sabin type 3 |

**India's routine schedule** uses OPV (birth dose + primary series) with
**fractional-dose IPV (fIPV)** introduced nationally after a 2016
VDPV2 detection — 2 intradermal fIPV doses achieve higher seroconversion
than one full IM dose.

---

## AFP Surveillance {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Since polio itself is often silent, **Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP)
case reporting** is the surveillance backbone — any child with sudden
flaccid paralysis is investigated, whether or not polio is suspected
clinically.

- **Sensitivity target:** ≥1 non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children
  under 15 detected annually — proof the system is sensitive enough to
  catch a real case if one occurred
- Two stool specimens, 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis
  onset, shipped to a WHO-accredited lab within 72 hours
- **Environmental surveillance** (testing sewage, e.g. in Mumbai) can
  detect circulating poliovirus even without a clinical AFP case

---

## Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus and India's Eradication {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

- **VDPV** — the live OPV strain, in communities with low vaccination
  coverage, can genetically revert over prolonged circulation and cause
  paralysis indistinguishable from wild-type polio; classified as
  circulating (cVDPV), immunodeficiency-associated (iVDPV), or ambiguous
  (aVDPV)
- **Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI)** — India's mass campaign strategy
  since 1995: two immunization rounds 4–6 weeks apart, during the
  **low-transmission season** (Nov–Feb), targeting every child under 5
  regardless of prior immunization status, as extra doses supplementing
  (not replacing) routine immunization

**Outcome:** India was certified **polio-free on 27 March 2014**. Wild
poliovirus type 2 (eradicated 2015) and type 3 (eradicated 2019) are
gone globally; type 1 is the only wild strain still circulating anywhere.

## Self-Check: Question 1 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

Approximately what proportion of poliovirus infections result in
paralysis?

- 50%
- 10%
- [1%]{.correct data-explanation="Only about 1% of poliovirus infections involve the CNS and cause paralysis — the overwhelming majority are subclinical, which is exactly what makes AFP surveillance and environmental surveillance necessary."}
- 25%
:::

---

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

Which vaccine induces intestinal (mucosal) immunity and can create herd
immunity through community spread of the vaccine virus?

- IPV
- [OPV]{.correct data-explanation="OPV, as a live attenuated oral vaccine, replicates in the gut, inducing secretory IgA (intestinal immunity) and spreading to contacts — producing herd immunity at roughly 66% coverage. IPV induces only humoral immunity."}
- Fractional IPV alone
- Human normal immunoglobulin
:::

---

## Self-Check: Question 3 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 3

The minimum surveillance sensitivity target for AFP case detection is:

- At least 1 case per 1,000 children under 15 per year
- [At least 1 non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children under 15 per year]{.correct data-explanation="This is the WHO benchmark used to confirm a surveillance system is sensitive enough to detect a true polio case if one occurred, even in polio-free settings."}
- At least 1 case per 10,000 children under 5 per year
- Zero AFP cases reported annually
:::
